claims.text: The AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock was previously processed under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing regimes.
Conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi generates high residual stresses.
Conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi produces a non-uniform microstructure.
An in-situ substrate-preheating window of 600–750 °C is applicable to miniature AlCrFeNiSi builds.
A machine-learning model can dynamically optimize substrate-preheating parameters during fabrication.
Substrate preheating at 600–750 °C will reduce abrupt thermal gradients in the melt pool.
Reducing abrupt melt-pool thermal gradients will allow more controlled solidification.
Substrate preheating will moderate the cooling rate.
A moderated cooling rate will reduce thermal-contraction stresses.
A moderated cooling rate will promote more uniform grain refinement during solidification.
ML-optimized substrate preheating will produce significantly lower residual stresses than conventional high-power processing without preheating.
ML-optimized substrate preheating will improve tensile strength relative to conventional high-power processing without preheating.
ML-optimized substrate preheating will extend fatigue life relative to conventional high-power processing without preheating.
Conventional high-power additive manufacturing without substrate preheating typically causes degraded mechanical performance.
The proposed comparison will keep processing parameters, build geometry, and environmental factors other than preheating constant.
Residual stress, tensile strength, fatigue life, grain size, and phase uniformity will be measured in preheated and control builds.
Failure to obtain statistically significant residual-stress reductions and mechanical-property improvements will refute the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field attributes prior additive-manufacturing processing and resulting residual stresses to the powder feedstock, whereas the other fields treat the powder as the input and residual stress as a property of the fabricated components.
